html:
The Quechan, or Kwatsáan, are a Yuman-speaking people of the lower Colorado River, around where the Gila River joins it near today's Yuma, Arizona. The Spanish called them Yuma.

Each year the river flooded, and when the water fell they planted maize, beans, squash and melons in the wet soil. They also fished and gathered mesquite beans. They held the river crossing that linked Sonora with California, and were rivals of the Cocopah and the Maricopa, and allies of the Mojave.

Juan Bautista de Anza crossed their land with Quechan help in 1774. When Spanish settlers and missions arrived, the Quechan rose in 1781, destroyed them and closed the overland route to California for decades. During the Gold Rush the crossing became a busy ferry, and the US Army built Fort Yuma in 1850. See also Yuma.
